clue.text: Distressed at the end of the school term?

definitions.text: at the end of the school term

blocks.note: first meaning: emotionally shattered, upset

blocks.clueFragment: at the end of the school term
blocks.note: second meaning: British schools are said to break up when term finishes for the holidays

explanation.surface: A pupil feels low as the holidays arrive, or a teacher worn out by the last day of term.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a school 'breaks up' for the holidays, so pupils on the last day have literally broken up.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for being emotionally shattered and also describes a school whose term has finished.

clue.text: Spot for parking inside? Yes, possibly

indicators.note: inside tells us one piece sits within the other letters
possibly suggests the word may be arranged some other way than as written

blocks.note: taken as written
P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether there is a parking space indoors and gets a hopeful reply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spot for parking' reads as a car space, but Spot is a verb and the definition stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To espy is to catch sight of something, a literary synonym for seeing or noticing.

clue.text: A lieutenant bearing one star

blocks.note: taken as written
Lt is the standard military abbreviation for lieutenant
an air is a manner or bearing, as in an air of confidence

explanation.surface: A junior officer wears a single star as a badge of rank.
explanation.walkthrough: The star looks like an insignia on the lieutenant's uniform, but it is a real star in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Altair is the brightest star in the constellation Aquila, one of the stars of the Summer Triangle.

clue.text: Swimmer who will leap ahead when detailed

definitions.text: Swimmer who will leap ahead when detailed

blocks.clueFragment: Swimmer who will leap ahead when detailed
blocks.note: surface reading: an athlete who will surge into the lead once given precise instructions
setter's reading: de-tailed, having lost its tail, when this young swimmer turns into a jumping frog

explanation.surface: A swimmer is promised to race into the lead once the coach has briefed them in detail.
explanation.walkthrough: Detailed means 'with its tail removed': the young swimmer loses its tail and becomes a frog that leaps.
explanation.definitionFit: A tadpole is the aquatic larva of a frog, which absorbs its tail as it develops into a hopping adult.

clue.text: Repeated invitation to adopt a more reasonable attitude

definitions.text: Repeated invitation to adopt a more reasonable attitude

blocks.note: surface reading: a summons issued twice over, a word of welcome said again

blocks.clueFragment: to adopt a more reasonable attitude
blocks.note: setter's reading: the doubled exclamation used to urge someone to calm down and be sensible

explanation.surface: Someone is asked twice over to be more sensible about things.
explanation.walkthrough: The invitation word is literally said twice, which is exactly how the remonstrating exclamation is formed.
explanation.definitionFit: The doubled exclamation is an idiom of mild reproof, telling a listener to stop being silly and behave reasonably.

clue.text: Official club servant

blocks.note: a mace is a heavy club used as a weapon
a bearer is a servant who carries things

explanation.surface: An employee of a club who works in an official capacity, like a steward at a golf club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Club servant' suggests a steward at a private club; club is the weapon instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A mace-bearer is a ceremonial officer who carries the mace before a mayor or in parliament.

clue.text: Robin getting two ducks? Bad luck!

blocks.note: Robin Hood, the outlaw of English legend
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, so O, and two of them make OO

explanation.surface: A batsman named Robin is out for nought in both innings, which is a cruel stroke of fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a duck is a score of zero, so it gives the round letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoodoo is a jinx or run of misfortune, something that brings ill fortune.

clue.text: Blair is changing note in foreign capital

indicators.note: changing means the letters are altered into a different arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
A is one of the notes of the musical scale

explanation.surface: Prime Minister Blair is altering a diplomatic note while visiting a capital abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changing note' looks like one phrase about a diplomatic message; the note supplies a letter and changing works on all of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Brasilia is the purpose-built capital city of Brazil, so a capital from abroad.

clue.text: He gives people his address

blocks.note: surface reading: someone handing out his home address to others
setter's reading: an address is a formal speech delivered to an audience

explanation.surface: A man readily tells people where he lives.
explanation.walkthrough: Address means a formal speech here, not a street location.
explanation.definitionFit: An orator is a public speaker, someone who delivers speeches to an assembled audience.

clue.text: Certainly nothing to chatter about

indicators.note: about means turned around, so this word is read back to front

blocks.note: O looks like zero, nothing
to yak is to chatter idly

explanation.surface: Someone says there is definitely nothing worth gossiping over.
explanation.definitionFit: As a reply, okay expresses agreement, much like saying yes or sure.

clue.text: Detains suspects

blocks.note: first meaning: arrests, takes into custody
second meaning: fears or anticipates something unpleasant

explanation.surface: The police hold people under suspicion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspects' reads as a noun, the people arrested, but it is a verb meaning fears.
explanation.definitionFit: To apprehend is to arrest someone, and also to anticipate something with dread or understand it.

clue.text: Moor in Arabian chorus

indicators.note: in tells us the letters sit within the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A Moorish figure appears singing among a group of Arab choristers.
explanation.walkthrough: Moor looks like a North African person, matching Arabian, but it is a verb about securing a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: To anchor a vessel is to fix it in place, the same as mooring it.

clue.text: Forester's hero -- an angry motorist?

blocks.note: first meaning: Horatio, the naval officer in C. S. Forester's novels
second meaning, whimsical: a driver who keeps sounding the car horn

explanation.surface: A woodsman's idol turns out to be a road-raging driver.
explanation.walkthrough: Forester is the novelist C. S. Forester, not a woodsman. The question mark flags the playful second reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Horatio Hornblower is the fictional Napoleonic-era captain; literally, the name describes someone honking a car horn.

clue.text: Regarded as having taken no active part

blocks.note: first meaning: considered, as in being viewed as a friend
second meaning: watched as a bystander without intervening

explanation.walkthrough: The phrasal verb works both as 'considered (as)' and as 'watched passively'.
explanation.definitionFit: A spectator merely watches, and the phrase also means viewed or considered someone in a certain light.

clue.text: Cut and run

blocks.note: first meaning: perform surgery on a patient
second meaning: work or manage a machine or business

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut and run' is an idiom for fleeing, but each word is a separate definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Surgeons perform surgery on patients, and people also work a machine or manage a business, both senses of the verb.

clue.text: School supplier folds before Spring

blocks.note: tucks are folds stitched into fabric
to hop is to spring or jump

explanation.surface: A school outfitter goes out of business ahead of the spring season.
explanation.walkthrough: Folds reads as 'goes bust', and Spring as the season; both are ordinary nouns here. A tuck shop is a British school's sweet and snack shop.
explanation.definitionFit: A tuck shop sells snacks and sweets to pupils on school premises, so it supplies a school.

clue.text: It is bound to show the titles

definitions.text: It is bound to show the titles

blocks.clueFragment: It is bound to show the titles
blocks.note: surface reading: something certain to display headings or names of works
setter's reading: a bound book, a reference volume that lists holders of noble rank

explanation.surface: Something is sure to put the titles on display, like credits at a film.
explanation.walkthrough: Bound means put between covers, not certain; Debrett's and Burke's are such books listing the nobility.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the nobility collectively and a book listing every lord and lady with their titles.

clue.text: Traffic jam in more ways than one

definitions.text: Traffic jam in more ways than one

blocks.note: surface reading: vehicles stuck nose to tail on a road
setter's reading: a jam spreading through several roads at once, locking a whole street grid

explanation.surface: A traffic jam bad enough to block several roads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In more ways than one' is a pun: the jam blocks traffic heading in several directions across a road network.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes a total standstill of vehicles across intersecting streets, where no car can move.

clue.text: Security is lifted in the store

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifted means read upwards, so the letters run backwards
in tells us one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: a depot is a storehouse
taken as written

explanation.surface: Valuables held as security are stolen from a shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Lifted reads as stolen, but in a down answer it sends the word upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A deposit is money paid as a guarantee, a security held against damage or default.

clue.text: French beard and pigtail, say, put on for the party

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the word and take a spelling of the same sound

blocks.note: barbe is the French word for beard
a queue is a plait of hair hanging down the back, a pigtail

explanation.surface: Someone dons a false French beard and pigtail as fancy dress for a party.
explanation.walkthrough: A queue is an old word for a pigtail; its sound is spelt as the billiards cue.
explanation.definitionFit: A barbecue is an outdoor social gathering where food is grilled over an open fire.

clue.text: Kept self-sufficient by a sum of petty cash

blocks.note: taken as written
a float is a small sum of cash kept for change or minor expenses

explanation.surface: A business stays independent with nothing more than a small cash fund.
explanation.definitionFit: Being afloat means staying solvent, financially able to keep going without help from others.

clue.text: It is feared leader is missing in RAF raid

definitions.note: used adjectivally: in a state of fear

indicators.note: the leader being missing means the opening letter is dropped

blocks.note: taken as written, a raid by the Royal Air Force; that the shortened run of letters also sits inside the phrase is a coincidence of the deletion

explanation.surface: It is feared that the squadron commander has been lost on a bombing mission.
explanation.walkthrough: Leader looks like the squadron's commanding officer, but it is just the first letter of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Afraid describes someone frightened, full of dread, the condition of being fearful.

clue.text: I start to become a model employer

indicators.note: to become signals the letters turning into something else by being rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone resolves to begin acting as an ideal boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model employer' suggests an ideal boss; read literally it is someone who employs models.
explanation.definitionFit: A painter or sculptor hires people to sit or pose for them, so is an employer of models.

clue.text: Initiates left in fox-hunting?

blocks.note: to blood a newcomer is to initiate them, originally by smearing them with a kill's blood
port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: Newcomers to the hunt are left out of the action.
explanation.walkthrough: Hunts traditionally 'blooded' a novice at their first kill, so the wordplay fits the definition's world. The question mark marks fox-hunting as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Fox-hunting is a classic instance of a pursuit in which animals are killed for sport.

clue.text: Quiet little chap making money

blocks.note: p (piano) is the musical direction for quiet
an elf is a small mythical being

explanation.surface: A quiet small man is earning a living.
explanation.definitionFit: Pelf is an old, usually disparaging word for wealth or riches, especially dishonestly gained.

clue.text: Design a tailless aircraft

indicators.note: tailless means the final letter is cut off

blocks.note: the article stays out of the answer; it is read with what follows
a plane is an aircraft

explanation.surface: An engineer draws up an aircraft without a tail section.
explanation.definitionFit: A plan is a scheme or drawing, as is a design for a building or machine.

clue.text: Manage to assemble a party

blocks.note: to make is to put together or construct
a do is an informal word for a party or celebration

explanation.surface: Someone succeeds in getting a party organised.
explanation.definitionFit: To make do is to get by or cope with whatever limited resources are available.

clue.text: An example of how one golfer differs from another?

definitions.text: how one golfer differs from another?

blocks.note: first meaning: a case or illustration

blocks.clueFragment: how one golfer differs from another?
blocks.note: second meaning, split in two: golfers vary in the way they stand to address the ball

explanation.surface: Someone asks for a case illustrating what sets one golfer apart from another.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as IN STANCE: golfers differ in their stance, the position of feet and body at the ball.
explanation.definitionFit: An instance is a particular case or occurrence cited as an illustration.
